awd_titl_txt: Workshop on Emerging Observational Needs in Atmospheric Chemistry; Boulder, Colorado; June 16-18, 2025
awd_abstract_narration:
A planning workshop will be held for the atmospheric chemistry community to discuss the future instrumentation needs of the community as part of the Lower Atmospheric Observing Facilities. The Lower Atmospheric Observing Facilities are managed by the National Center for Atmospheric Research and administered by University Corporation for Atmospheric Research. The facility provides instruments to the atmospheric science community for use in field campaigns or in other observational studies. This workshop will bring together the research community to focus on emerging needs in lower atmosphere observational capabilities that will lead to scientific advances in atmospheric chemistry and Earth system science.

The goals of the meetings are: (1) Discuss the community’s observational needs now and into the future with an emphasis on the NSF Lower Atmospheric Observing Facilities and the Community Instruments and Facilities; (2) Improve communication and knowledge about atmospheric chemistry observational research activities being conducted by university PIs and scientists supported by the NSF-Atmospheric Chemistry Program and scientists supported at NSF sponsored facilities; (3) Encourage new and continued collaboration between NSF-Atmospheric Chemistry Program-supported PIs and NSF facility scientists; and (4) Develop a widespread understanding in the community of the atmospheric chemistry observational activities and community facilities available at NSF supported centers. The workshop will be held June 16-18 in Boulder Colorado. It will serve to initiate a direct dialogue between all participants, to inform each other of current scientific activities, to discuss future observational needs and to develop plans for future research and collaborations.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
This award supported a workshop that brought together researchers and facility managers from NCAR, universities, and partner agencies to assess the state of atmospheric chemistry observational infrastructure supported by the National Science Foundation. The workshop gave NSF and the community it supports a clear picture of current priorities and future directions for observational needs in atmospheric chemistry, evaluating current capacity across instruments, airborne platforms, and laboratory facilities, and identifying priority investments needed to sustain and advance the nation's ability to measure atmospheric composition, clouds, aerosols, and radiation. Community Instruments and Facilities (CIF) were introduced and discussed although the majority of the workshop time was spent on airborne observational science activities and outlook.

Discussions confirmed that the current national research aircraft fleet--the NSF/NCAR GV, a C-130-class aircraft, and a University of Wyoming King Air--serve distinct and complementary scientific roles and together generally meet the community's current needs, with each platform providing unique access to different parts of the troposphere and upper troposphere/lower stratosphere. Participants examined the broader set of community instruments and facilities available through the Lower Atmosphere Observing Facilities (LAOF) program, and through the CIF program including specialized cloud chamber, mountain laboratory, and ice nucleation research facilities, and discussed recent science motivating new observational needs. Breakout sessions addressed LAOF and university/community instrument capabilities across radiation and meteorology, trace gases, aerosol chemistry and microphysics, cloud chemistry and microphysics, and surface fluxes, with detailed recommendations to be disseminated in a forthcoming community report.

A central finding was that the airborne program's success depends on a tightly interactive ecosystem between university investigators and NCAR scientists, built around a core set of community-requestable instruments maintained by personnel funded through NSF and other agencies; participants agreed that NCAR and the university community cannot sustain current instrument capabilities through core NSF funding alone. The workshop also weighed the trade-offs between community-requestable and investigator-driven instrumentation, concluding that some instruments are appropriately investigator-led and should remain so. Participants further noted that economies of scale available at NCAR--where a single engineer can maintain multiple instruments--are not available at universities, and that current capabilities at both NCAR and university facilities are at or near minimum requirements, placing some community capabilities at risk. The group agreed that identifying and addressing at-risk infrastructure early is essential to ensure continuity of the airborne program, and that a dedicated program supporting the testing of new instruments on airborne platforms, preferably with an educational component, would be highly valuable.

The workshop highlighted the urgent need to sustain a pipeline of trained instrument scientists, recommending expanded internship and training opportunities for graduate students working directly with instrumentation to address a growing gap in engineering and technical continuity at universities and national facilities alike. It also strengthened coordination between NCAR, university investigators, and other federal agencies, including a commitment to a cross-agency effort addressing the potential loss of whole-air-sampling capability. By synthesizing input from a broad segment of the atmospheric chemistry community, the workshop produced actionable recommendations that will guide future NSF and NCAR investment decisions, helping ensure continued public access to shared national research infrastructure--aircraft, community instruments, and laboratory facilities--that supports nationwide university-led science.
